newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-ROMANCE FLOURISHES IN OPENING F.A. CUP ROUND.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ROMANCE FLOURISHES IN OPENING F.A. CUP ROUND.

text.p: Football fan Michael Hutton will never score the winning goal in an F.A. Cup final.
But he must have felt just like a Cup winner when minor league Hendon visited third division Cardiff City on Saturday.
At halftime in their first round match at Ninian Park Michael asked his girlfriend Lorraine over the public address system to marry him .
There was a nervous silence and anxious looks as 2,500 Welshmen, women and children waited while Lorraine, after a pause, said: "Yes, I will."

The cheer that went up for the happy couple bedecked in Hendon's green-and-white colours from a couple of thousand Welsh strangers, was as loud as the roar that greeted the two goals Cardiff scored to knock their rivals out of the competition.

Hendon's dreams of Wembley, or at least, a third round tie at Manchester United, may be over for another year but for Michael and Lorraine, the day they became engaged will be one they will never forget.
The same goes for all the part-time players who battled through as many as five qualifying rounds to play their part in one of English soccer's most romantic days.

More than 500 part-time clubs enter the world's oldest and most famous club cup competition every year. In the middle of November the 32 survivors from the qualifying series mix it in the first round proper with the 48 teams in the lower two English league divisions.
The premier league and first division teams stay out of the firing line until the third round in January.
Surprisingly for once, none of the 18 minor league teams who faced League opposition won, but seven forced replays and were at least included in the draw for the second round made on Saturday.

A sprinkling survived from matches between minor league sides, so the bricklayers, estate agents, teachers, former professionals and double-glazing salesmen who form the backbone of clubs like Northwich Victoria, Boston United, St Albans, Colwyn Bay and Sudbury Town, can dream of Cup glory for a while yet.
So can boxing promoter Barry Hearn, chairman of third division strugglers Leyton Orient, who came from a goal down against Welsh part-timers Merthyr Tydfil to win 2-1.
"I've put on fights for Nigel Benn and Chris Eubank, but the F.A. Cup is far more demanding," said a relieved Hearn afterwards.

Merthyr are managed by Colin Addison, once of Atletico Madrid, Vigo Celta and Cadiz. He was also the inspirational player-manager at then non-League Hereford United when they scored one of the greatest shocks in the competition's 125-year history by beating first division Newcastle United in 1972.

Addison is planning a 25th anniversary re-union dinner to mark that famous victory next January, but Hereford's current team, hovering near the bottom of the third division, had nothing to celebrate on Saturday, losing 1-0 to Gillingham.

Brighton, who were in the F.A. Cup final 13 years ago but are now facing extinction and are bottom of the third division, managed to survive a scare at Sudbury, based in a small town in Suffolk which happens to be the biggest silk centre in Europe. They were held 0-0, the result written up in chalk on the blackboard outside the dressing rooms afterwards.
In an F.A. Cup match at Sudbury last year, play was held up after the ball was lost in a hedge. A far-from silky Brighton were lucky to escape with a replay.

Plenty of publicity surrounded Newcastle's appearance in the first round for the first time , albeit Newcastle Town rather than United. The Newcastle that played Notts County are based in the Midlands and usually appear in front of 50 fans and a dog.

But last week their goalkeeper faced shooting practice from United's Les Ferdinand and United's assistant coach Terry McDermott sent them a good luck message before they played Notts County at Stoke's ground. Unfortunately, help from their Geordie namesakes was not enough and Notts County won 2-0.
It was left to Kevin Ratcliffe, an F.A. Cup winner with Everton in 1984, to sum up every pragmatic League manager's nightmare on a day laden with dreams.
Ratcliffe now manages third division Chester who brushed past Stalybridge Celtic, a League team for two seasons 80-odd years ago,.
"With so many non-League teams in the first round there is going to be an upset -- we've got to make sure it is not us," he said before the start.
Afterwards Chester were drawn against minor league Boston in the second round and an elated Ratcliffe said: "I'm just happy to be in the hat for the next round."

He knows that with one more victory the prospect of Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal or Tottenham providing the opposition becomes a reality. And for all true supporters like Hendon's Michael and Lorraine, there's no end to dreaming about what can happen then.
